newsitem.title: UK: Bumblebee flying could aid aicraft design.
newsitem.headline: Bumblebee flying could aid aicraft design.

text.p: Any good scientist knows insects should not be able to fly -- their bodies are too fat for their tiny wings to lift.
But an expert on aerodynamics and insect flight said on Wednesday he had solved the mystery and come up with data that will fascinate aircraft designers.

Reporting in the science journal Nature, Charles Ellington said insects create a complex pattern of vortices when they flutter their wings. Ellington said he had mapped out this pattern for the first time.
Each vortex acted to lift the insect up into the air.
"They increase the lift because they are a region of low pressure and that is acting to suck the wing upwards, creating lift force," he said in a telephone interview.
Experts knew this must be happening. They just did not know how.
Ellington and his colleagues used a hawkmoth -- a large moth that moves its wings relatively slowly and thus would be easier to study. Its wing movement is typical of many insects.
They tethered the moth with thread inside a small wind tunnel and blew smoke into it. They photographed the patterns made by the smoke as it passed over the wings of the frantically flapping moth.
They then constructed a mechanical model of the moth that was much bigger and flapped more slowly, while still accurately modelling the motion of the wings.

They were amazed to see a complicated pattern of loops and spirals spinning away from the wings. Just as one vortex died out -- which would create an effect known as stalling, making the bug (or aircraft) plunge earthwards -- another vortex would kick in and stabilise it.
"This is so unlike what we had expected all along that this is a shock, really," Ellington said.
His findings could probably be applied to aircraft design, he said, especially helicopters which also use vortices to create lift.

"The first thing I did when we discovered this was turn to the literature on aerodynamics on rotary wings, helicopters, propellers and things like that because they have the same type of aerodynamics," he said.
But nothing had been written about such effects. "It's something we are going to start looking at," he added. "It's a way to get something like two or three times more lift."
Other experts said the findings could shed light on the mysteries that still surround bird flight.
"It remains to be discovered whether similar effects occur in the flapping flight of birds," commented R McNeill Alexander, an expert in biomechanics at the University of Leeds.
